course_title: Indigenous Politics within and beyond the state
course_description:
This course examines the relationship between Indigenous and mainstream conceptions of political community, sovereignty, power, policy, rights, diplomacy and conflict to question, reflect, and expand upon dominant understandings of (international) politics. These themes are examined in the context of the development of transnational Indigenous activism in the late 20th Century and the challenges of ongoing conflicts between Indigenous peoples and settlers in settler-colonial societies. The course will increase your understanding of Indigenous peoples, advance creative thinking about alternative ways of constituting and maintaining political order, and enhance capacities for working across cultural difference.

Welcome to POLS7190!

First Nations peoples have constituted and practised political orders long before the emergence of civilisations that are usually taken as the starting points for prevailing approaches to and reflections about politics. And although colonialism has inflicted incredible damage upon Indigenous societies, Indigenous peoples have in recent decades re-gathered and remobilised in local, national and international fora, including through United Nations processes connected with the adoption of the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples. Despite these developments, a range of political and policy challenges persist, from issues of contested sovereignty and Indigenous-Settler relations to challenges of policy development and service delivery. Scholarship on these and related topics is changing, with Indigenous politics a burgeoning and challenging topic in political science and related disciplines.

In this course, taught in an interactive seminar mode, you will the opportunity to examine the issues posed by Indigenous politics. The course will challenge and enlarge upon conventional conceptions of politics and introduce you to creative ways of thinking about key political issues and challenges.

course_aims:
To develop an understanding of Indigenous conceptions of politics in comparison with predominant Western approaches.

To reflect critically upon how dominant approaches to politics and policy - as well as their implementation - impact upon Indigenous peoples.

To advance creativeﾠthinking about alternative and innovative political relations and policy approaches between Indigenous peoples and states.ﾠ

learning_outcomes.description: Identify Indigenous and predominant western approaches to politics at play in political relations, in policy frameworks and strategies, and in contested or conflictual political debates.
Understand key historical dynamics and relations between Indigenous peoples and states/mainstream populations.
Identify possible pathways and practices for improving political relations and policy-making between Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples.
Critically reflect upon how existing knowledge is disrupted, confirmed or extended amid the contestations that accompany knowing about Indigenous politics.

assessment_details.other_conditions: Time limited, Secure. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Task You are to complete a 150 word (approximately) relflection on the seminar discussion each week (excluding weeks 6 and 13). You will be expected to discuss how your understanding of the topic is evolving, how your interpretaton of the reading/s have changed during the discussion, and how your learning is progressing. To complete this task you should engage with a) at least one of the required readings and the pre-recorded video, b) the class discussion (comments and interpretations of your colleagues and course staff) and c) the course Learning Outcomes while reflecting upon how you are coming to know. Rather than aiming primarily to demonstrate what you know, you should also engage in self-analysis and critique. Your reflection is to be answered individually in handwritten form in class. Paper will be provided. No electronic devices are permitted to be used. Your final mark for this item will be based upon your best 8 contributions. Course staff will guide and support you to participate in this novel form of assessment. They will advise you on how to prepare you for this task, and provide you with additionional in-class prompts to help focus your reflection. If a medical or other circumstance leads to challenges for you completing this assessment item, please contact the course coordinator directly. Please consult the criteria sheet for this item. Background Participation in the seminars is an essential part of this course and is directly linked with the course Learning Outcomes (see Aims and Outcomes section). Our best learning often happens through reflection. This can occur when we consider the challenges of knowing amidst contested political relations, are open with ourselves and others about the processes that accompany our learning, and reflect upon how our existing knowledge is disrupted, confirmed or extended. Consider, for instance, that our relationship with knowing can be emotional. Learning may be challenging, confronting, affirming, surprising, or frustrating. You should aim to openly discuss these and other experiences in engaging with the topic (including readings and pre-recorded videos) with your class colleagues, and link these with your experience of learning. Please Note: This assessment task is to be completed in person. The use of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) or Machine Translation (MT) tools will not be permitted. Any attempt to use AI or MT may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. Read full task description Hide full task description

assessment_details.task_description: Task You are required prepare a 1200 word written document to a) identify an audience for one of the topics outlined in the 'Issue Analysis and Commentary paper: Topics and guidance' document, b) design an aligned communication strategy for your paper, and c) make a structured plan for your paper. You should explain who you are targeting and why they are a relevant target for your chosen topic, specify your strategy for communicating the complexity and challenge implicit in your topic to the target audience, and map how you will structure content to inform and persuade your audience. You should aim to structure your document using headings to reflect the three core components. Please consult the criteria sheet for this item. Background Effective communication regarding complex matters requires careful strategic planning. Understanding your audience and devising an effective communication strategy is especially important. This task is designed to help you prepare for the final assessment task, the Issue Analysis and Commentary Paper. assessment_details.title: Issue Analysis & Commentary Paper (1800 words)
assessment_details.other_conditions: Student specific. See the conditions definitions
assessment_details.task_description: Task You are to conceptualise, prepare and submit an Issue Analysis and Commentary paper. Possible topics and guidance are listed in the relevant Blackboard folder (there is an option to develop your own topic). Depending on the work you have done in the previous assessment item, you may be writing for a government minister, informing a leader in a non-government organistion, or informing the work of an advocacy organisation. Your submission should aim be balanced and informed by argumentation and evidence (including existing scholarship) yet not at the expense of avoiding challenging or contentious matters. This is a text-based assessment; your submission should contain no images. Remember to build upon your work in the Planning Document and to carefully target your audience. Please consult the Marking Criteria for this item. Background Researchers and advocates use written texts to inform and persuade decision-makers and policy-makers, sometimes by advocating for their or their constituents' or point of view. The targeted policy- and decision-makers are often - but not always - politicians and public servants. These texts are variously called discussion papers, options papers, policy briefs, issue briefs and other terms too. There are no exact rules about how these types of texts are constructed, but they usually have key goals of raising a challenging or complex issue, condensing the issue into a brief and accessible format, and advocating for a reasoned and/or evidence-based response in relation to the issue. This assessment item builds on the Planning Document. learning_activities.topic: Week 1 - Position, Place, Relation Introduction to the course and each other. Individual positioning in relation to land, ways of knowing, political relations, study area, and particular topics/interests.
Week 2 - First Encounters, Identities, Definitions Patterning of early encounters, conceptualisations of identity, and definitions of Indigenous people/s.
Week 3 - Colonisation, Occupation, Decolonisation Bases for colonisation, patterns of rule, movements for decolonisation.
Week 4 - Bureaucracy, Culture, Racialisation Policy development and operation in relation to Indigenous peoples.
Week 5 - Treaties, Agreements, Negotiations Challenges and possibilities of negotiations and treaties.
Week 6 - Class documentary movie and dialogue Viewing of Dhakiyarr Vs the King , and dialogue about experience of learning in the class to this point. Learning outcomes: L01, L02
Week 7 - Law, Justice, Rights Divergent and overlapping conceptions of justice and law, and the place of law in pursuit of justice and rights
Week 8 - Conflict, Diplomacy, Peace Modes of conflict management and diplomacy, intercultural challenges and opportunities
Week 9 - Land, Resources, Place Securing existence, divergent approaches to land and resources
Week 11 - State, Sovereignty, Nation Foundations and conceptualisations of political authority and ordering.
Week 12 - Cosmology, Knowing, Being Positioning the human, foundations of existence and ways of knowing Learning outcomes: L01, L02

Week 13 - Conclusion/Dialogue Affirming or unsettling the state? Exploration of questions raised by the course, revisiting individual positioning in relation to personal/professional interests. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03
